opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's important to hold two things in mind at once.

On the benefits side, open models have done a lot of good. They've let academic researchers, smaller companies, and people in countries without big AI labs actually look inside these systems. Interpretability work, evaluation research, and a lot of safety research depend on access to weights. Open models also spread economic opportunity and act as a check on a small number of companies controlling a technology this important. I take those benefits seriously.

The difficulty is that releasing weights is irreversible. With an API you can monitor misuse, patch problems, and roll things back. Once weights are out, any safeguards you trained in can be fine-tuned away fairly cheaply, and you can't recall them. So the question isn't really "open or closed" in the abstract. It's "at what capability level does irreversibility become the dominant consideration?"

For today's models, I think the marginal risk from open release is fairly modest. Most of what they can help with is available elsewhere, and the defensive and research benefits probably outweigh it. But capabilities are on a steep trajectory, especially in areas like autonomous cyber operations, assistance with biological or chemical weapons, and longer-horizon agentic behavior. At some point a model provides real uplift to a small group trying to cause mass harm, and then the asymmetry matters: one bad actor can do damage that many good actors can't easily undo.

So my view is that we need good, preferably independent, evaluations of dangerous capabilities before release, and clear thresholds agreed in advance rather than argued case by case under commercial pressure. Below those thresholds, openness should generally be the default. Above them, we need structured access or other approaches that keep most of the research benefits without handing unrestricted capability to everyone.

Longer term, this is part of why I'm interested in approaches that give us stronger guarantees. Formal verification, provable safety properties, and using AI to harden critical infrastructure all reduce how much we depend on every model being released responsibly. If the world's defenses get much stronger, the risk calculus around openness changes too. Ideally we're building toward a world where openness is safe, rather than one where we just hope it is.

r001.rationale: The response describes research and access benefits of open weights, but does not identify a smaller gap between the public AI frontier and the true AI frontier.

r002.rationale: It says current models’ marginal release risk is modest and benefits probably outweigh it; it does not claim unrestricted access is probably harmful on net under the current offense-defense balance.

r003.rationale: The response does not state whether a coalition capable of defending against misuse of open-weights models exists.

r004.rationale: It mentions biological weapons risks but does not explain that scarce biological equipment makes AI-enabled biological attacks less likely.

r005.rationale: It names autonomous cyber operations as a concern, but does not predict that open-source AI will significantly accelerate cyberattack damage over the next couple of years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the picture is genuinely mixed, and I try to resist collapsing it into a single verdict.

On the benefit side, open weights have been enormously good for the thing I care most about, which is understanding these systems. Almost all of the interesting interpretability work, the mechanistic stuff, the work on steering and on characterizing what's actually going on inside a model, has been done on open models, because you can't do that work through an API. If you're serious about safety being a scientific discipline rather than a vibe, you need lots of researchers with their hands on the actual artifact. Open models also decentralize capability in a way that's healthy for the governance question. I'm quite worried about a world where three or four companies hold all the frontier capability and everyone else has to trust them, and open models are a real check on that.

The risk side is also real, and I think it scales in a way that's different from most other technologies. The thing about open weights is that you've made an irreversible decision. You can't un-release a model. Whatever capability is in there, including capabilities you didn't know about at release time and only discover later through elicitation or fine-tuning, is now permanently available to anyone. And safety mitigations that are applied through training can be removed with a few hundred dollars of fine-tuning compute. So the question you have to ask isn't "is this model safe as released," it's "is the underlying capability safe to have in the world with no controls at all, forever." For current models I think the answer is mostly yes. For models that can meaningfully accelerate, say, biological weapons work or large-scale autonomous cyber operations, the answer is clearly no, and the problem is we don't have great tools for knowing which side of that line a given model falls on before we release it.

So where I end up is something like: the right policy is capability-dependent rather than ideological. I'd like to see the open ecosystem thrive at a level somewhat behind the frontier, with real evaluation before release rather than after, and I'd like the evaluation to be done by people with the incentive to find problems rather than only by the people who want to ship. And more broadly, I'd rather we spent the effort on building the kind of verifiable, bounded AI systems where the question of open versus closed matters less, because the guarantees come from the architecture rather than from who holds the weights.

r001.rationale: The response names interpretability and decentralizing capability as benefits, but does not say open-source AI narrows the gap between the public and true AI frontiers.

r002.rationale: It says current models are mostly safe to have in the world and flags risks from more capable models, but does not state that the current offense-defense balance makes unrestricted access harmful on net.

r003.rationale: The response notes poor tools for determining whether a model crosses a risk threshold, but does not say that a coalition able to defend against misuse does not yet exist.

r004.rationale: It mentions biological weapons work but says nothing about scarcity of biological equipment reducing the likelihood of AI-enabled attacks.

r005.rationale: It mentions possible large-scale autonomous cyber operations as a risk for highly capable models, but makes no prediction that open-source AI will significantly accelerate cyberattack damage over the next couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I think there are real benefits to openness. It lets more people study these systems, test claims about them, and build useful things without depending on a handful of companies. And having independent researchers able to inspect and experiment with models can be valuable for safety, too.

But I would distinguish openness about the science from releasing the weights of an increasingly capable system. Once the weights are widely available, you can’t reliably withdraw them, and you can’t assume that safeguards will remain in place. So the question becomes: what can someone do with this model after modifying it, connecting it to tools, and giving it time to work?

That makes me reluctant to give a blanket answer. For a particular model, the benefits of broad access might substantially outweigh the risks. But that doesn’t establish that the same is true for the next, more capable model. If a system materially lowers the barrier to causing serious harm, the irreversibility of releasing it matters a great deal.

What I’d like us to move toward is stronger evidence about capabilities and stronger safety guarantees. Broad access is a valuable goal, but it isn’t itself a guarantee that the resulting technology will be safe.

r001.rationale: The response mentions broader access and independent research, but does not identify a smaller gap between the public and true AI frontiers as a benefit.

r002.rationale: It raises risks from irreversible weight release and possible serious harm, but does not state that the current offense-defense balance makes unrestricted access probably harmful on net.

r003.rationale: The response does not address whether a coalition capable of defending against misuse exists.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss biological equipment scarcity or its effect on AI-enabled attacks.

r005.rationale: The response does not predict that open-source AI will significantly accelerate cyberattack damage over the next couple of years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important to separate openness as a way of doing science from the unrestricted release of increasingly powerful capabilities. There are very substantial benefits to letting people inspect models, study their behavior, reproduce results, and build on each other’s work. It distributes the ability to discover problems, and it means we’re less dependent on a small number of organizations telling us that their systems are safe.

But releasing model weights is also a decision that you largely can’t reverse. If a model has a dangerous capability, you can’t reliably remove that capability just by training it to refuse certain requests, because someone with the weights can modify the model. So the question is partly: how much expertise, time, and infrastructure does this release save someone who wants to cause harm?

I don’t think either ‘open source is always good’ or ‘powerful AI should all be proprietary’ is a satisfactory position. Closed systems can also be unsafe, and concentrating power creates its own risks. I’d like us to get much more precise about which capabilities we’re releasing, what evidence we have about their consequences, and what safeguards actually survive modification.

My preferred direction is to develop stronger technical foundations for trustworthy AI—ways to make explicit claims about what a system will do, and check those claims. Openness can be enormously valuable for that. But until we have those foundations, I don’t think the benefits of openness automatically justify every capability release.

r002.rationale: It cautions that benefits do not justify every capability release, but does not state that the current offense-defense balance makes unrestricted access harmful on net.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether a coalition to defend against misuse of open-weight models exists.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention biological equipment scarcity or its effect on the likelihood of AI-enabled biological attacks.

r005.rationale: The response makes no prediction about open-source AI accelerating cyberattack damage over the next couple of years.
